Release a narrow repair-status service on the approved Django/Postgres stack. Preserve the sponsor’s accessible tenant status page and agent updates. Defer SMS and automatic tradesperson scheduling; agents coordinate tradespeople manually.

For the first release, agents can create a repair request, update its status and next action, and publish a tenant-facing update. Tenants can securely view their own request’s current status, last update, next step and agency contact. Keep internal notes private. Use a small, explicit status vocabulary and show when an update is overdue. Limit rollout to one agency and existing repair requests; defer attachments, reporting dashboards and integrations.

Allocate the ten engineering days to the core flow, access controls, accessibility checks and release validation. Agree scope on day one and review delivery risk halfway through. Cut optional breadth or reduce the rollout cohort if needed, while preserving both promised capabilities. Release only after tenant isolation, keyboard use and screen-reader reading have been checked.

There is no measured baseline, so the interviews establish a problem hypothesis, not an improvement claim. Before rollout, sample recent repairs to record status-chasing contacts per request and time since the last meaningful update. During a two-week pilot, measure those same outcomes, agent update completion and tenants’ ability to identify the current status and next action. Record denominators and compare similar repair stages. Page views are diagnostic, not success.

Agree provisional improvement targets and an acceptable agent workload with the sponsor before rollout. Stop release for access-control or accessibility failures. Reshape the pilot if agents cannot sustain updates, tenants still cannot understand progress, or status-chasing does not improve. Investigate the coordination process before adding automation.
